title: The pears (Confessions 2)
hookLine: young Augustine steals pears he doesn't want, just for the thrill

lines: A PEAR TREE BY A VINEYARD.
cards: A pear tree, next to a vineyard, loaded with fruit. And the pears, Augustine tells us, weren't even good: nothing special to look at, nothing special to eat.
We step back a book now, to Book Two of the Confessions, when he's still a boy at home. Late one night, after hanging around the streets, he and a gang of friends go to that tree. They shake it.
They haul off armloads of pears. They aren't hungry. They don't want pears.
Long afterward, as he writes, this small theft is still bothering him.

teach.h: NOT HUNGRY, NOT EVEN GOOD PEARS.
teach.b: Here's what they did with the pears. They ate a few, Augustine says, and threw the rest to the pigs. He had better pears at home.
So why? That's the whole question of the passage, and he won't let it go. The only pleasure in it, he says, was that it wasn't allowed.
He loved not the pears, but the wrong itself. Then he goes looking for a motive the way a detective would.
People who do terrible things, he says, usually want something: another man's wife, his land, money to live on, revenge. Even a cruel man has a reason. He can't find his.

teach.h: ALONE, HE WOULDN'T HAVE DONE IT.
teach.b: He would not have done it alone. Alone, he says, it would have been no fun at all. It was the laughing together, the dare, the being in on it.

He calls it a friendship that was no friend at all. Some readers hear an echo of another garden here, the tree in Genesis, fruit taken because it was forbidden. The loads were heavy, he says, but the stakes were nothing.
Pears nobody wanted. Pig food. That's why it works.
A big crime has big reasons.

teach.h: A SMALL WRONG SHOWS THE HEART.
teach.b: A pointless wrong shows the heart with nothing else in the way.
And notice the tone. No list of punishments, no big drama. He's asking, in front of God, a question that's easy to skip: why did I do it?

how: Catholics prepare for confession with an examination of conscience, looking back over what they have done and why; Augustine's Confessions is read as an example of that kind of honest look.

games.q: you're out late with your friends. someone points at a neighbor's pear tree. the pears aren't even good. what happens?
o: you shake the tree, haul off the pears and throw them to the pigs.
you eat one pear and leave the rest.
games.why: that's what Augustine and his friends did. the point wasn't the pears; it was that it wasn't allowed.

practice: Not your worst moment: let one small wrong come up, with no good reason behind it, a cruel joke, something broken for fun, a rumor passed on because it was juicy.
Ask Augustine's question quietly, why did I do it, who was I with, what did I want, and don't punish yourself; just look. If you pray, name it to God, the way Augustine did.

wordCard.voice: The pears. A small theft from Augustine's boyhood, pears he didn't want, taken with friends for the thrill of the forbidden. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: why did I do it. An honest question, asked gently and without punishment. Until tomorrow.
